analysis.one_liner: Requires large livestock farms to follow approved animal waste plans to keep manure out of water.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after Senate hearings in April 1998, it sat in the Agriculture Committee until the Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required large, concentrated livestock and poultry operations to get a US Department of Agriculture-approved waste management plan before they could operate or expand. Plans would have had to keep animal manure out of streams and groundwater, cap how much nitrogen and phosphorus could be spread on fields, ban dumping waste on frozen or saturated ground, set construction standards for manure lagoons, and hold the big companies that own the animals responsible even when contract farmers raise them. Smaller farms were exempt and could get federal cost-share payments to adopt voluntary plans.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near large livestock operations and communities downstream: their water, wells, air, and property are the ones affected by manure runoff, lagoon leaks, and odors. Small farms also benefit from $600 million a year in authorized conservation payments for voluntary waste plans.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Rural residents near large livestock farms

how_it_helps.text: Existing large operations could not legally run after 18 months without an approved animal waste management plan, and new or expanded operations could not be built without one [S3].
Plans had to prevent discharges of animal waste into surface and groundwater and include containment design standards, leak contingency measures, and nutrient testing [S3].

Spreading manure was prohibited where it would exceed crop nitrogen and phosphorus needs or threaten water pollution or soil toxicity, and was banned on ice, snow, frozen, or water-saturated soil [S3].

Earthen lagoons located below the water table, in unsuitable soils, too close to wells and streams, or unlined would have been barred, with emergency shutoff and failsafe capacity required for liquid waste systems [S3].
Contract language could not shift legal responsibility for pollution from the company that owns the animals to the farmer who raises them [S3].
The Agriculture Department could have modified or revoked plans and compelled closure of operations without approved plans [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large livestock and poultry companies and big feedlot operators, who would bear the cost of plans, inspections, containment construction, and treatment of excess waste, plus taxpayers for the authorized conservation spending.

drawbacks.text: Compliance would have been expensive: approved plans, on-site inspections, lined lagoons, and treatment or covered storage of excess waste all cost money, and operators warned-style concerns about higher meat prices are fair to acknowledge; those costs would largely fall on large operations, not small family farms, which were exempt [S3].

Putting the Agriculture Department rather than the Environmental Protection Agency in charge of a federal waste permit program could mean enforcement weaker than the Clean Water Act regime, and the bill authorized open-ended appropriations on top of $600 million a year for conservation payments [S2],[S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and local: less manure in drinking water, streams, and wells near factory-scale farms, and liability that sticks to the big animal owners rather than washing off onto contract growers. The costs are real but concentrated on the largest operations, whose waste is the stated problem; the main design weakness is relying on USDA rather than EPA for enforcement. On balance a well-aimed bill whose costs land mostly where the pollution comes from.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, got a hearing in April 1998, and then nothing: no committee vote and no floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin introduced the bill on October 28, 1997, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry [S5].
The committee held a hearing on April 2, 1998, printing S.Hrg. 105-953 [S5].
No markup, committee vote, or Senate floor vote ever followed; the bill's last recorded action is that hearing [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill died in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large livestock and poultry operations are better off: they never faced a federal permit requirement, lagoon construction standards, application limits, or owner liability for waste from contract farms, and rural communities near those operations kept bearing the pollution risk.

for.name: Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it; it was referred to the Agriculture Committee [S5].

for.name: One Democratic cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsor it attracted [S4].

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Held a hearing on April 2, 1998 but never reported the bill out or voted on it, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so party positions are hard to read; the bill's two sponsors were both Democrats, and the Republican-run committee that held a hearing never advanced it [S4],[S5].

industries.industry: Large livestock and poultry integrators and feedlot operators
industries.note: The bill would have required federal-approved waste plans, upgraded and lined manure lagoons, restricted manure spreading, and kept legal liability with the companies that own the animals even when farmers raise them under contract. Its rules bite hardest on operations above 200,000 pounds of animal capacity, while exempting small farms [S3].
Farms below the concentrated-operation threshold are exempt from the mandate and would have qualified for $600 million a year in environmental cost-share payments to adopt voluntary waste plans [S3].

Plan development, inspections, containment construction, and nutrient testing would have created demand for conservation technical services, supported by the expanded environmental quality incentives program funding [S2],[S3].
